passage:
I'm Joseph, and I shared a flat with Ira in our second year of college in Pune. I still remember the night in October.
I woke to a strange sound. Ira was sitting on the kitchen floor, gasping, her hands clawing at her chest. "I'm dying," she kept saying.
My own heart started hammering. I wanted to scream for the neighbours. Instead I sat down across from her, not too close, and made my voice slow. "I'm here. You're safe. Breathe out with me." I said it again and again, feeling anything but calm inside.
It passed. She cried, and I made us both tea.
The next morning I didn't just leave it. I walked with her to the campus health centre and waited outside. Looking back, I think my steadiness mattered more than any words.

qa.q: Where was Ira sitting when Joseph woke up?
qa.a: On the kitchen floor.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel while helping Ira?
qa.a: Joseph felt scared, heart hammering and wanting to scream for the neighbours, but chose to stay slow and steady on the outside.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that other roommates could learn from?
qa.a: Stay close but not crowding, speak slowly and kindly as an anchor, and follow up the next day by going with the person to get care.

qa.q: How might Ira have experienced Joseph's steady voice?
qa.a: She probably felt less alone and had something to hold on to while she was terrified.

grounding: Joseph sees roommate Ira gasping and terrified, feels scared too, stays steady and kind as an anchor, and follows up with care the next day.

subtype: Rituals to keep bad things away [Actor]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4, from Bhavna Joshi.
For the past few weeks I've noticed Nandini washing her hands many times before lunch until her knuckles are red and cracked. Before sitting, she touches each corner of her desk. Today she whispered "safe, safe, safe" under her breath before opening her tiffin.
When I asked gently, she said, "If I don't, something bad will happen to Mummy." Her eyes filled. She said she knows it sounds silly but she can't stop.
I didn't scold her or tell her to stop. I told her I believed her that it felt very hard. I called her mother after school the same day, and we agreed she would talk to the school counsellor, who suggested a child psychologist. Nandini seemed calmer after I sat with her.

qa.q: What did Nandini whisper before opening her tiffin?
qa.a: "Safe, safe, safe."

qa.q: How does Nandini feel about her rituals?
qa.a: She feels frightened that something bad will happen to Mummy, and stuck, because she knows it sounds silly but can't stop.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next that helped the family?
qa.a: The teacher stayed calm, didn't scold, believed Nandini, and called her mother the same day to involve the counsellor and a child psychologist.

qa.q: What would change if the teacher had scolded Nandini?
qa.a: Her fear and shame would probably grow, and she might hide the rituals, making them worse.

grounding: A teacher notices Nandini repeating handwashing, touching and words to prevent harm, avoids scolding and helps the family reach a counsellor and child psychologist.

passage:
Monday. "Mumma, is the door locked?" Divyansh, nine, asked at bedtime. "Yes." "Are you sure?" "Yes, beta." He asked eleven times. Each time, Mumma answered, and each time he calmed a little, then asked again. She also waited outside the bathroom while he washed his hands.
Three weeks later. The questions had doubled. Mumma had changed the whole morning so he could check his school bag four times. They were late for the bus twice. She loved him so much, but she was exhausted.
The next Saturday. Dr Farhan, the child psychologist, listened to her. "You answer because you love him," he said gently. "But each answer teaches his worry that it needs one more. Let's plan how to support him without feeding the worry." Together they wrote a plan: one answer, then "I already told you, I believe you can handle this."

qa.q: How many times did Divyansh ask about the door on Monday?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: How was Mumma feeling three weeks later?
qa.a: She felt loving but exhausted and worried, with the questions doubling and the family late for the bus.

qa.q: What did Dr Farhan suggest instead of answering every time?
qa.a: Giving one answer, then calmly trusting Divyansh to handle the worry, so the pattern isn't fed and strengthened.

qa.q: What is it like for Divyansh when the questions keep coming?
qa.a: He feels anxious and only briefly calmer after each answer, so he needs to ask again and again.

grounding: Mumma answers Divyansh's repeated questions and changes routines out of love, which strengthens the pattern, and a clinician advises how to help without feeding it.

passage:
Wasim: Api are you awake
Preeti: Yes. What's up?
Wasim: I need to tell you something but you'll hate me
Preeti: I won't. Promise.
Wasim: I keep getting horrible thoughts. Like pictures of hurting people I love. I'd never ever do it. I hate them. They just pop in.
Wasim: Does that mean I'm a bad person?
Preeti: No, bhai. Thank you for telling me. I read that lots of people get thoughts like that. The fact that you hate them shows who you really are.
Wasim: I've been scared for months. Too ashamed to tell anyone.
Preeti: That sounds so lonely. Ammi's still up. Can I come to your room and we tell her together now? A counsellor can really help with this.
Wasim: Okay. Come.
Preeti: Coming.

qa.q: How long has Wasim been scared?
qa.a: For months.

qa.q: Why did Wasim keep the thoughts secret?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid that the thoughts meant he was a bad person, so he told nobody.

qa.q: Which of Preeti's replies helped most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Wasim such thoughts are common and don't show who he is, then going with him that night to tell Ammi and seek a counsellor, which broke the secret and the shame.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt reading Wasim's messages?
qa.a: She probably felt concerned and tender, glad he trusted her and eager to get him support.

grounding: Wasim has upsetting intrusive thoughts he fears mean he is bad, and his sister reassures him they are common and helps him seek help.

passage:
You were late again, Vijay, and I saw you go back to check your scooter lock three times. So let me tell you something your Rajni Mausi has never told anyone in this family.
When I was twenty, in my college hostel, I began checking the iron was off. Once, then five times, then twenty. Then the taps, then the window latch. Each check gave me one sweet second of relief. Then the fear came back bigger, wanting more.
I missed my first class most days. My friends thought I was lazy. I told them I overslept. It was easier than the truth.
One day I stood at the door for an hour and cried. That evening I told my roommate, and the next week I saw a psychiatrist at the college hospital. It took a long time, beta, but it got smaller. So if this is you, don't hide it the way I did.

qa.q: How long did young Rajni stand at the door that day?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: How did young Rajni feel after each check?
qa.a: Young Rajni felt a brief second of relief, then the fear came back bigger, wanting more checks.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rajni Mausi's story?
qa.a: Telling a roommate and seeing a psychiatrist at the college hospital, instead of hiding the checking from friends.

qa.q: How might young Rajni's friends have seen things back then?
qa.a: They thought Rajni was lazy and oversleeping, never guessing the fear being hidden.

grounding: Rajni Mausi tells Vijay how, at twenty, hours of checking caused lateness that was hidden from friends, with relief bringing more fear, until a qualified clinician was sought.

passage:
It was Diwali week in their colony in Jaipur, and crackers went off every few minutes. For Ira, eight, it was the hardest week since the fire in their old house last winter.
Every bang made her jump and grab the nearest hand. At night she woke screaming. In the afternoons she played the same game with her dolls: the house burns, the dolls run, the house burns again. When Dadaji lit the diya, she went silent and stared at the wall.
Dadaji didn't tell her to be brave. He kept her day the same: bath, lunch, story, nap. He sat by her bed at night, saying, "You are safe. Dadaji is here." He closed the windows to muffle the noise.
After Diwali, he and her mother took her to a child specialist the school had suggested. On the way, Ira held his hand tight.

qa.q: What game did Ira play with her dolls?
qa.a: The house burns, the dolls run, the house burns again.

qa.q: How does Ira feel when the crackers go off?
qa.a: She feels startled and frightened, jumping and grabbing the nearest hand because the bangs bring back the fire.

qa.q: What did Dadaji do that helped Ira feel safe?
qa.a: He kept her routine the same, stayed with her at night, reassured her, muffled the noise, and took her to a child specialist.

qa.q: How might Dadaji feel watching Ira stare at the wall when the diya is lit?
qa.a: He probably feels worried and sad, but he stays calm and patient so she can trust him.

grounding: Ira startles at loud sounds, has nightmares, replays scary scenes and shuts down after a fire, and safety, routine, a trusted adult and a child specialist help.

passage:
It had been two months since the school bus accident, and exam week had come with pouring rain. Farhan and Naveen had both been on that bus.
In the exam hall, a truck horn blared outside. Farhan froze, pen stopped mid-word, eyes blank. He didn't hear the invigilator call his name.
Naveen jumped too, but differently. When a classmate joked, "Scared of a horn?" Naveen shoved him hard and was sent out.
At home Farhan had become the perfect son, agreeing to everything, never saying no. His mother thought he was fine.
That Friday the school counsellor met both boys. "Freezing, going numb, lashing out, trying to please everyone, these are ways your body tried to keep you safe," she said. "They're not signs that you're bad or weak." Naveen looked up, surprised. Farhan's shoulders dropped for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What sound made Farhan freeze in the exam hall?
qa.a: A truck horn blaring outside.

qa.q: How was Farhan feeling in the exam hall?
qa.a: He was frightened and went numb, frozen and blank, not even hearing his name.

qa.q: What did the counsellor explain that could help both boys?
qa.a: That freezing, lashing out and pleasing everyone are protective survival responses after something frightening, not character faults.

qa.q: How might Farhan's mother see him differently after learning this?
qa.a: She might realise that his constant agreeing was a way of staying safe, not proof that he was fine.

grounding: After a bus accident, Farhan freezes, goes numb and pleases everyone while Naveen lashes out, and a counsellor explains these are survival responses, not faults.

passage:
I'm Nilesh, the students call me Nilesh Sir, and I teach Class 9 maths. Let me tell you about Saurabh.
Last year he'd explode over tiny things. A dropped pen, a changed seat. Other days he'd go silent and stare. The old me would have said, "What's wrong with you?" in front of the whole class.
Instead, one day after class, I asked, "What happened this year, Saurabh?" Not what's wrong. What happened. He was quiet, then said his family lost their home in the monsoon flood. They were living in a relief camp for a while.
So I changed some things. Same seat every day. I write the plan on the board each morning, no surprises. I never corrected him in front of others. And I referred him to our counsellor, with his parents' agreement.
He still has bad days. But he stays in the room now.

qa.q: What happened to Saurabh's family's home?
qa.a: They lost their home in the monsoon flood.

qa.q: How did Nilesh Sir feel when Saurabh first exploded over small things?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and tempted to snap back, but he chose curiosity and concern instead.

qa.q: Which of Nilesh Sir's changes helped Saurabh, and why?
qa.a: Asking what happened, a fixed seat, a daily written plan, no public correction and a counsellor referral made class predictable and safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh when his seat is suddenly changed?
qa.a: It probably feels alarming and unsafe, bringing back the upheaval of losing his home.

grounding: Nilesh Sir sees a student explode or go silent over small things, asks what happened, sets predictable routines, avoids public shaming and refers him to a counsellor.

subtype: Feeling unsafe in a safe place [Actor]
passage:
Six months after she was mugged on the way home in Valencia, Camila still took the long route, avoiding that street. She sat facing the door in every café. When a scooter passed close, her whole body jerked.
Her flatmate Dalia invited her to a party. Camila went, stood in the corner, and felt like she was watching everyone through glass. When a stranger touched her arm to pass, she flinched so hard her drink spilled. She went home ashamed.
"I should be over this by now," she told Dalia. "I'm just weak."
Dalia sat beside her. "You're not weak. You're safe now, but your body doesn't believe it yet. Willpower alone won't fix that."
The next week Camila booked a session with a therapist at the university who worked with people after frightening events. She told Dalia afterwards, "It's going to take time. But I think I can trust her."

qa.q: What did Camila do when a stranger touched her arm?
qa.a: She flinched so hard her drink spilled.

qa.q: How did Camila feel going home from the party?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and detached, like she was watching everyone through glass, and blamed herself as weak.

qa.q: What did Camila do that could help her heal?
qa.a: She stopped relying on willpower alone and booked sessions with a trained therapist, accepting that it would take time.

qa.q: How does Dalia see Camila's reactions?
qa.a: Dalia sees them as her body still not feeling safe, not as weakness, and feels caring and patient.

grounding: Camila feels on edge, avoids reminders, feels detached and ashamed and struggles to trust after a mugging, and seeks time, safety and trained support.

passage:
Seema came up behind Nandini at the Andheri bus stop and put a hand on her shoulder. Nandini spun round, pushed her away and stood shaking.
"Sorry, sorry," Seema said, stunned. They had been friends since school.
Later that week Nandini cancelled their movie plan and stopped replying. Seema felt confused and a little hurt. What had she done?
She didn't push. On Sunday she texted, "I'm not asking about anything. I just want to know what helps you."
Nandini replied that evening. "Don't come up behind me. Tell me before you touch me. And please don't ask about last year. I'm working on it with my counsellor."
"Done," Seema wrote. "I'll wait till you're ready, or forever."
The next week Nandini met her for chai. Seema said, "Hi, I'm right here," before sitting down. Nandini smiled.

qa.q: Where was Nandini when Seema put a hand on her shoulder?
qa.a: At the Andheri bus stop.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when Nandini cancelled and stopped replying?
qa.a: She felt confused and a little hurt, wondering what she had done.

qa.q: Which of Seema's choices created safety?
qa.a: Not pushing for details, asking what helps, respecting Nandini's pace and following her requests, like announcing herself before sitting down.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Seema after the Sunday text?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and trusts Seema more, admiring how she respects her pace without asking questions.

grounding: Seema is confused when Nandini pulls away and reacts strongly, and patience, asking what helps and respecting her pace without pushing for details create safety.
